intro_en: The Israel National Trail descends to the lowest place on earth. Along the way we look out over Masada from a less familiar angle and see the Dead Sea from the fault escarpment. We finish on the Ein Bokek hotels promenade along the evaporation ponds.
character_en: (For those walking north to south) A short climb at the start, followed by easy walking to the top of Ma'ale Mor. On Ma'ale Mor the trail descends about 300 metres in elevation, on a long and relatively gentle descent. The final stretch, at the foot of the fault escarpment and along the salt-pond promenade, is gentle.
transport_en: At the start point - none. At the end point - the Ein Bokek hotels
important_en: When there is a flash-flood warning for the Judean Desert streams, hiking is prohibited and dangerous.
For those wishing to include a visit to Masada, there is an entrance fee to the site.
description_en:
We set out from the western parking lot of Masada, at the foot of the siege ramp. We descend south on a red-marked trail into the northern tributary of Nahal Metzada. Nahal Metzada drains the southern part of Masada, as opposed to Nahal Ben Yair, which drains its northern side, and it is the stream that fed and filled the mountain's lower cisterns. The watershed between the two tributaries runs along the siege ramp built by the Romans.
We walk at the foot of Masada, west of the mountain, with the saddle of Mount Elazar visible ahead of us to the south. The trail passes above the waterfall of Nahal Metzada and climbs to the saddle on a short ascent.
At the saddle it is worth pausing, turning to look north and seeing Masada from a less familiar angle. There is a fine view here of the siege ramp and of the southern side of the Masada mountain, with the remains of the casemate wall built around the summit at its top. The saddle itself is crossed by the circumvallation wall (dyke) that the Romans built around the mountain during the siege, and you can follow the line of the wall as it continues ahead of us above the channel we walked along. The wall also climbs to the summit of Mount Elazar above us.
If time allows, it is worth lingering a little longer in the area and making the short climb to the top of Mount Elazar on the black-marked trail. From the top of the mountain you can see the remains of one of the eight camps the Romans built during the siege of Masada, and enjoy a broader view over Masada and its surroundings, the Dead Sea and southwards to the southern Judean Desert plateau.
After a short descent heading south, the Israel National Trail leaves the red marking and continues in the same direction on a black-marked trail. We walk a short stretch on a green-marked jeep track, then return to a black-marked trail.
The trail descends into the channel of Nahal Rahaf and crosses the channel over a short distance, before the stream enters a canyon with waterfalls. It is worth going a short distance down the channel to see the start of the canyon. Caution: do not go beyond the point where the stream begins cutting into the hard rock and the first waterfall comes into view.
Here you can find a shady corner for a break - almost the only opportunity along this segment. There is a good chance that guests will join the break: Tristram's starlings, black birds that call with a melodious whistle. Tristram's starlings are named after the English clergyman Tristram, who toured and studied the country in the mid-19th century. These visitors, hoping to enjoy the leftovers of your meal, will pounce on every breadcrumb or scrap of fruit.
From the channel we make a short climb back up to the desert plateau. After a short distance the trail meets the two entrances to Ma'ale Rahaf - blue and green. The trail continues on the black trail south to the top of Ma'ale Mor. From here, together with a red-marked trail, we descend the fault escarpment into the Dead Sea rift, the lowest place on earth.
Ma'ale Mor follows an ancient route that chose to "overcome" the fault escarpment at the point where the edge of the desert plateau and the top of the ascent are at the lowest level on the rim of the cliff. The course of Ma'ale Mor is divided into 3 steps, giving hikers stretches of gentle walking between the sections of descent - which makes it one of the easiest ascents between the Dead Sea and the desert plateau.
From the top of the ascent and along it there are fine views over the Dead Sea rift - the northern basin, the Lisan peninsula, the evaporation ponds, and on the other side of the rift the rising Mountains of Moab.
At the bottom of the ascent, the trail crosses the channel of Nahal Mor and continues south between the fault escarpment and Road 90. As the trail approaches Nahal Ye'elim, it turns west towards the cliff in order to enter the stream's channel comfortably.
On entering the stream, we follow the channel east to beneath the bridge that carries the road. After a short walk over a stone surface laid to stabilise the surroundings of the bridge during floods, we reach the end of the retaining wall standing on our right and leave the channel for the promenade. The promenade runs along the edge of the northern evaporation pond of the Dead Sea Works and reaches the entrance to the Ein Bokek hotel complex. Here, beside the roundabout, there is a plaza on the water's edge that serves as an overnight campsite - an organised spot for sleeping out in the hotel area.
Recommended lodging in the area
Masada West overnight campsite - a lodging spot with a shower, for a fee. Requires advance arrangement with the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) (telephone 08-6280404, extension 1).
nearby_en: Ein Bokek - Nahal Bokek, a short flowing-water route, free of charge.
Points of interest: Masada, Mount Elazar. The channel of Nahal Rahaf. The top of the fault escarpment. Ma'ale Mor. The hotels promenade along the evaporation ponds.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
